9-panel cinematic storyboard sheet derived from Image 1. Mix Wide, Medium, and Tight shots of the same scene. No borders between panels.

Layout: 3x3 grid (9 panels) in a 16:9 landscape image.

Scene: Extreme macro beauty still, modern social-first editorial photography, 16:9. SCARLETT in her pale kiosk uniform polo shirt, collar loose and hem half-tucked into denim cutoff shorts, an elastic hair tie on her wrist, framed so tightly that only her mouth, chin and the sharp line of her jaw fill the frame in three-quarter profile. She is drinking straight from a dented stainless steel water bottle, lips parted and pressed to the metal rim, mid-swallow, one bead of water breaking loose and tracking down her chin toward her throat while the back of her wrist rises into the lower edge of frame, tendons tensed, an instant from wiping it away. Coral-painted mouth still perfectly intact, glossy and unsmudged. Sunlight rakes hard across the skin from the upper right, carving a crisp bright edge along the jawline and throwing the far side into deep soft shadow, tiny water droplets on the bottle's brushed steel throwing pinpoint specular flares, condensation slicking the metal. Behind her the glossy white-painted timber counter ledge of a beachside kiosk service hatch blows out into a bright creamy blur, the shallow dark slot of the kiosk interior a soft black wedge, a smear of warm yellow from a sweating paper cup of frozen pineapple and a suggestion of an aluminium sliding window frame dissolving in bokeh. Warm true-to-life grade, crisp whites, lifted airy shadows, coral as the single accent pop against neutrals. Shot handheld with natural micro-shake on a 100mm macro lens at f/2.0, razor-thin depth of field holding only the lower lip and chin, subtle skin texture and fine sun-bleached down catching the light, natural grain, no diffusion.

Every panel is a shot of the same scene as Image 1 — keep the characters, wardrobe, lighting, color grade, and texture consistent across all panels.

No text, dialogue bubbles, scene numbers, or watermarks.

Reference images define identity — keep every referenced character, object, and location consistent with its reference image; never render a reference image itself as a separate panel or subject.
